questions.question: What is the difference between a thread and a process, and why does it matter?
questions.title: Threads vs Processes
questions.direct_answer: A process is an instance of a running program with its own memory space; a thread is a unit of execution within a process that shares that process's memory with other threads. Processes are isolated (one crashing doesn't affect another) but heavy to create and communicate between (IPC). Threads are lightweight, fast to create and switch, and share memory (easy data sharing) but are not isolated (one thread's crash can bring down the process) and need synchronization to avoid races. The trade-off: isolation vs lightweight sharing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the isolation-vs-sharing trade-off: processes are isolated (safe but heavy); threads share memory (light but need synchronization).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'threads are smaller processes' without naming the shared-memory consequence (need synchronization) and isolation difference.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Processes have separate memory (isolated, heavy, IPC); threads share a process's memory (light, easy sharing, need synchronization, not isolated). Trade-off: isolation vs sharing.

sections.title: Isolation vs Sharing
sections.content: A process is an instance of a running program with its own private memory space; a thread is a unit of execution within a process that shares that process's memory with other threads. Processes are isolated — one crashing doesn't affect another — which makes them safe but heavy to create and communicate between (you need IPC: pipes, sockets, shared files). Threads are lightweight, fast to create and context-switch, and share memory, which makes data sharing easy but means they're not isolated (one thread's crash can bring down the whole process) and they need synchronization (locks, atomics) to avoid races. The fundamental trade-off is isolation versus lightweight sharing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Saying 'a thread is a small process' — missing the shared-memory consequence (needs synchronization).
Forgetting that shared memory is fast but unsafe without synchronization (races).
Assuming threads are isolated like processes — they're not; one crash can kill the process.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A process has its own memory; a thread shares its process's memory with other threads.
Processes are isolated (crash-safe) but heavy; threads are light but not isolated.
Threads share memory (easy data sharing) but need synchronization to avoid races.
Inter-process communication (IPC) is needed between processes; threads just share memory.
The trade-off is isolation vs lightweight sharing.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A process is an instance of a running program with its own private memory space, and a thread is a unit of execution within a process that shares that process's memory with other threads. Processes are isolated — one crashing doesn't affect another — which makes them safe but heavy to create and communicate between, requiring IPC like pipes, sockets, or shared files. Threads are lightweight, fast to create and context-switch, and share memory, which makes data sharing easy but means they're not isolated — one thread's crash can bring down the whole process — and they need synchronization, like locks or atomics, to avoid races. The fundamental trade-off is isolation versus lightweight sharing. A common mistake is saying a thread is a small process, which misses the shared-memory consequence that threads need synchronization, and assuming threads are isolated like processes, which they're not — one thread's crash can kill the whole process.
